angle: Why did a painting of a shipwreck embarrass the French government?
answer: The Méduse was wrecked under a captain who owed his post to the restored king; the survivors' book exposed mutiny and cannibalism, and Géricault painted it with forensic realism, calling it only 'Scene of a Shipwreck' though everyone knew which; he chose the moment the rescue ship was vanishing, when hope could still fail.

script.text: That speck on the horizon is the whole point of this painting.
It's a ship, the first these men had seen in thirteen days.
So why did this shipwreck enrage the French government?
In 1816, the frigate Méduse ran aground off West Africa.
script.say: In eighteen sixteen, the frigate May-dooz ran aground off West Africa.

script.text: Its captain owed his post to the king, and had barely sailed in twenty years.
So when the lifeboats cut the towropes, about 150 people were left on a raft.
But after thirteen days, only fifteen were alive.
Two survivors published what happened: mutiny, starvation, cannibalism.
So the wreck became a scandal for the king's government.
But Géricault, aged 27, wanted the horror exact.
script.say: But Zheri-ko, aged twenty-seven, wanted the horror exact.

script.text: He interviewed survivors and studied severed heads from a hospital.
His young friend Delacroix posed for this dead man, face down.
script.say: His young friend Della-kwah posed for this dead man, face down.

script.text: But look again at that speck: the real ship sailed out of sight.
It returned two hours later; he painted the moment hope might fail.
He called it simply Scene of a Shipwreck, and all Paris knew which.

post.caption:
That speck on the horizon is a rescue ship, and in real life it sailed out of sight. Géricault studied severed heads and had Delacroix pose as a corpse to paint the wreck France's government wanted forgotten.
Can you spot the ship?
